name: session_2026_04_09
description: Twelve snippets from merken's own design session on 2026-04-08/09. Six topics, two events each. Deliberately includes two borderline pairs (loop_philosophy, consolidation_design) whose embedding cosine sits right around the 0.65 default threshold — a known weakness we're tracking, not a bug to hide.

events.text: The user never asked to compete with mempalace; they just stumbled on it before starting and used it as a mirror to check their own architectural instincts.
User said mempalace is not the target — it's a reflection to learn from the architecture and avoid their launch failure mode.
The real target is building a local agent loop that decides when to remember, when to recall, when to consolidate, and when to forget.
User wants merken to be useful for their own loop first and then compare it with existing systems afterward.
HeuristicWriteDecider's exact-dedup rule never fires on LongMemEval because the haystacks have no duplicates.
The LongMemEval benchmark cannot validate merken's filtering logic; a different scenario-driven benchmark is needed.
A vstash UX bug was found: Memory.search() without a collection argument leaks results across all collections; issue 165 was filed upstream.
vstash.SearchResult does not expose tags or layer on recall hits, so metadata has to be smuggled via the title field.
The original dedup in HeuristicWriteDecider called vstash.search on every write, making ingest O(N squared) per haystack.
The recall-based dedup was replaced with an in-process set of normalized strings for exact matching, constant time per check.
Consolidation is additive, not destructive: episodic events stay raw and semantic facts are derived on top of them with provenance pointers.
The v1 consolidate pipeline uses embedding cosine clustering with threshold 0.65, no LLM, and records method=embedding_v1 on each fact.

queries.question: why did we not set mempalace as a target to beat?
what vstash bug did we find while building the audit log?
why was the dedup rule rewritten to use an in-process set?
what did we learn about LongMemEval as a benchmark for merken?
